overview: Merina royal centres developed in Madagascar’s highlands, a landscape of palaces, ancestral places and cultivated land. This card follows that particular political tradition, rather than treating every Malagasy community as Merina.

periods.title: Before the kingdom described here
periods.summary: The map uses the Merina name earlier than the royal history described on this page. Ambohimanga’s documented heritage principally represents the fifteenth to nineteenth centuries; the year 1000 is a map boundary, not a verified founding date.

periods.title: Highland royal places
periods.summary: Ambohimanga developed as a royal centre with sacred places and an agricultural landscape. This earlier history should be distinguished from the later expansion of a much larger kingdom.

periods.title: Andrianampoinimerina consolidates power
periods.summary: Andrianampoinimerina brought competing highland polities together. Irrigated rice, trading wealth, enslavement, family relationships and ritual authority all mattered in the kingdom’s formation; no single invention explains his success.

periods.title: Radama I and expansion
periods.summary: Radama I expanded toward coastal trade routes. British recognition and assistance strengthened his position, but a claim to rule Madagascar did not mean effective control of the entire island.

periods.title: Ranavalona I and state-directed production
periods.summary: Ranavalona I continued and enlarged policies of state monopolies, manufacturing and compulsory labour. Skilled Malagasy workers contributed to industrial production, while military expansion imposed severe burdens on conquered communities.

periods.title: Medical teaching in the capital
periods.summary: A mission hospital opened in Antananarivo in July 1865. Its work included training Malagasy doctors, nurses and midwives. This institution formed one part of the region’s varied history of healthcare.

periods.title: Ranavalona III’s reign
periods.summary: Ranavalona III became queen in 1883. The 1885 agreement with France left sovereignty contested: French claims to a protectorate did not amount to settled colonial control.

periods.title: Conquest and annexation
periods.summary: French troops took Antananarivo in September 1895 and imposed a new protectorate. France annexed Madagascar in August 1896. The queen remained temporarily before being forced into exile in February 1897.

periods.title: After the monarchy
periods.summary: French authorities removed royal remains from Ambohimanga and demolished its tombs in 1897. Pilgrimage continued despite those interventions. The map’s Imerina label through 1914 does not mean the independent monarchy survived.

sections.title: Opening the gate was a serious job

items.text: Ambohimanga had fourteen gateways belonging to different phases of its defences. ICOMOS describes doors weighing as much as twelve tonnes and carefully controlled access. These entrances displayed royal status as well as regulating movement. Forgetting something outside could be inconvenient on a scale far beyond having to find your house key.

Inside the royal enclosure were two basins cut into rock, connected with the annual royal bathing ceremony. The surrounding spaces included royal burial places and an area for public pronouncements. Water here had ritual significance. These surviving basins are evidence for a particular court ceremony, not a picture of how every highland household washed.

sections.title: Ironworking leaves a very durable mess

items.text: At Marorangotra, beside today’s Lake Mantasoa, researchers investigated heaps of slag, the waste left by making iron. They also found fragments of stone air pipes used in furnaces. The wider region was producing iron in the late nineteenth century, but the report does not establish when every deposit began. These are traces of skilled local production, not proof that ironworking arrived with European factories.

A small excavation at Marorangotra also recovered pieces of a large cooking pot with a black graphite coating, alongside animal bones including zebu cattle. Such finds put ordinary equipment beside industrial waste. They do not reveal a complete workers’ menu: the bones are not automatically one meal, and the report leaves the deposits’ precise dates unresolved.

In early nineteenth-century Antananarivo, school writing supplies could be scarce. One account describes smooth wooden boards rubbed with grease and dusted with ash. Pupils wrote with a wooden point, then wiped the marks away with a rag or finger. Reusable schoolwork did not require a battery, although keeping that board off your best clothes sounds sensible.

Students helped produce Malagasy translations rather than simply copying their foreign teachers. They carried word lists home on slates and consulted relatives about suitable expressions. Families thus contributed knowledge to work that later appeared in books. The teacher might know the English word, while a child and their household knew better how to say it in Malagasy.

The resulting work depended on people whose contributions were easily overlooked. An enslaved interpreter named Joseph helped missionary David Jones learn Malagasy. Larson’s research brings interpreters and pupils back into a history often told mainly through European missionaries’ names. Learning a language was a shared achievement, carried out within profoundly unequal relationships.

A Merina silk cloth in the British Museum, dated approximately 1875 to 1900, consists of two panels sewn together. Coloured stripes and floating threads create elaborate patterns. It belongs to a tradition of costly cloth associated with aristocratic dress and burial. Its arrival in the museum in 1969 is a collection date, not the date somebody wove it.

The museum describes nineteenth-century Merina weavers keeping designs on paper beside their looms. Extra thread controls helped them build bands of geometric decoration. That combination of a written plan and careful handwork makes the complexity easier to appreciate. The catalogue does not identify a secret meaning for every pattern, so a handsome zigzag need not become a mysterious code.

The Antananarivo mission hospital opened in July 1865 as part of Andrew Davidson’s medical work. Malagasy students learned medicine, nursing and midwifery, and medical material was published in Malagasy. Two trainees, Andrianaly and Rajaonah, later studied in Edinburgh. Their careers show local learners becoming practitioners, rather than patients being the only Malagasy people in the story.

The kingdom’s workshops made goods including glass and cannon, with Malagasy apprentices mastering new manufacturing techniques. But workers did not all choose their jobs. Fanompoana required unpaid labour for the state, and military conquest also enslaved people. Campbell’s history describes workers and soldiers fleeing harsh conditions. Achievements in production belong beside the experiences of the people required to produce them.

sections.title: A letter at the end of a reign

items.text: The British Library catalogues copies of a letter dated 27 February 1897 in which General Gallieni ordered Queen Ranavalona III’s exile. The surviving catalogue gives a precise documentary trace of a political turning point. These are photocopies preserved in an archive, not an excavated object, and the catalogue description is different from reading the original letter itself.

ending.text: French conquest in 1895 and annexation in 1896 ended the kingdom’s independence. Ranavalona III was forced into exile in February 1897, ending the monarchy. Merina communities continued under colonial rule. Neither the map’s change of label in 1878 nor its endpoint in 1914 dates this political ending.
